issues.legal_issue: A statutory vesting of forest land and rights to trees or their produce includes a separate right to cut trees held by a person other than the intermediary.
material_facts: An intermediary granted the appellant a contractual right to cut trees in demarcated forest areas, and that right remained with the appellant on the date of vesting.
A notification brought the relevant estate within the statutory vesting scheme.
The amendment expressly addressed forest land together with rights to trees or their produce held by an intermediary or any other person.
The appeal challenged the dismissal of a writ petition concerning the effect of the vesting scheme on the appellant’s right.
issues.conclusion: The right to cut the trees vested in the State even though it had been granted to and was held by a person other than the intermediary.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 5(aa) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, as inserted by the 1957 amendment, “together with” means “as well as” and enumerates property interests without requiring common ownership of the land and tree rights. “Held by an intermediary or any other person” encompasses separate interests in which the intermediary holds the land and another person holds the right to trees or their produce. The amendment’s purpose of overcoming earlier Calcutta High Court decisions is relevant where the text bears that construction. The absence of compensation does not detract from the clear operation of the provision.

rule.if: vesting_interpretation_appeal and notified_forest_estate and separate_tree_cutting_right and right_held_by_non_intermediary

predicates.vesting_interpretation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging how a statutory vesting scheme applies to a claimed property interest.
predicates.notified_forest_estate: A government notification has subjected forest land within an estate to vesting.
predicates.separate_tree_cutting_right: A right to cut trees in forest land is held separately from the interest in the land.
predicates.right_held_by_non_intermediary: A person other than the intermediary holds the tree-cutting right when vesting takes effect.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns notified forest land and a separate tree-cutting right held by someone other than the intermediary, the separate right vests in the State.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of compensation for an acquired interest does not narrow the clear scope of a statutory vesting provision.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the lack of a compensation provision for his tree-cutting interest meant that the interest was outside the vesting provision.
The Court found that the provision’s words plainly covered rights to trees held by a person other than the intermediary.
issues.conclusion: The absence of compensation could not detract from the clear operation of the vesting provision.
issues.legal_principle: Where the statutory words clearly include an interest, the absence of a provision compensating its holder does not justify construing the interest out of the provision. The Court distinguished the question of statutory interpretation from a possible constitutional challenge based on the absence of compensation.

predicates.vesting_interpretation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging how a statutory vesting scheme applies to a claimed property interest.
predicates.clear_text_covers_interest: The words of the vesting provision plainly include the interest in dispute.
predicates.compensation_not_provided: The governing law provides no compensation for the holder of the interest being acquired.

issues.definition: If clear statutory wording covers an interest, the absence of compensation does not narrow the provision’s reach.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of compensation does not by itself invalidate an acquisition under an enactment protected by its inclusion in the constitutional schedule.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the acquisition on the ground that no compensation had been provided for his tree-cutting rights.
The enactment had been included in the Ninth Schedule following the Seventeenth Amendment to the Constitution.
The appellant did not dispute that the absence of compensation would not render the enactment or acquisition unconstitutional after that inclusion.
issues.conclusion: The Court treated the constitutional challenge based on the absence of compensation as not requiring determination, given the appellant’s acceptance that the enactment’s inclusion in the Ninth Schedule prevented that ground from invalidating the acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the Seventeenth Amendment and the inclusion of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, in the Ninth Schedule. It recorded that, after that inclusion, the absence of compensation would not render the enactment or acquisition unconstitutional; the appellant did not contest that position.

predicates.constitutional_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the constitutionality of an acquisition.
predicates.enactment_in_constitutional_schedule: The law authorizing the acquisition is included in a constitutional schedule that protects it from the asserted challenge.
predicates.compensation_not_provided: The governing law provides no compensation for the acquired interest.

issues.definition: When an acquisition appeal concerns a law included in a constitutionally protective schedule, lack of compensation alone does not invalidate the acquisition.
